World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: 15yo among five people charged over alleged kidnapping of rapper's bodyguard
World.content:
A 15-year-old boy is among five people charged in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a rapper's bodyguard in Sydney's west.

Police said a 32-year-old man was allegedly assaulted and forced into a car outside a home in Guildford about 11:30pm on Monday.

A short time later the vehicle was found partially burnt-out in nearby Villawood.

About an hour later, heavily armed officers zeroed in on a property in Casula where they found the man with facial injuries.

The man allegedly kidnapped was Emilio Chalhoub, who is believed to be the personal bodyguard for rapper and alleged Alameddine associate Ali Younes, who performs under the name "Ay Huncho".

"Ay Huncho", aka Ali Younes, an alleged Alameddine associate who has been repeatedly targeted over the past year. (Four Corners: Nick Wiggins)

About 3:20am, detectives raided the Casula property and allegedly seized a firearm, baseball bat and other items.

Four men and a teenage boy were arrested and taken to Liverpool Police Station where they have since been charged.

A 22-year-old man from Blacktown was charged with kidnap in company with intent serious indict occasion actual bodily harm, participate and contribute to criminal group, possess unauthorised prohibited firearm, blacken or disguise face with intent to commit an indictable offence and destroy property in company use greater than $5,000.

The 32-year-old was allegedly assaulted then forcibly taken. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

A 21-year-old man from Queensland, a 21-year-old man from Macquarie Fields and a 22-year-old man were also handed charges.

They included kidnap in company with intent serious indict occasion actual bodily harm, participate and contribute in criminal group, blacken or disguise face with intent to commit an indictable offence, aggravated take or drive motor vehicle with person armed with weapon, possess unauthorised prohibited firearm and destroy property in company use greater than $5,000.

The four men were refused bail and are due to appear at Liverpool Local Court on Wednesday.

A 15-year-old boy will also face Children's Court on Wednesday on kidnapping offences.

His other charges include participate and contribute to criminal group, blacken or disguise face with intent to commit an indictable offence, aggravated take or drive motor vehicle with person armed with weapon, possess unauthorised prohibited firearm and destroy property in company use greater than $5,000.

World.title: 'Terrifying' experience for WA family as storm tears roof off their home
World.content:
A woman has described her terrifying experience after a powerful storm tore the roof off her family home while she was inside.

Western Australia's first major cold front for the year left a trail of damage throughout southern WA, including Esperance, with Rachel Corrin's home in East Bunbury, 170 kilometres south of Perth, gutted by the system.

The Bureau of Meteorology said there was not enough evidence to conclusively determine if the powerful system, which struck the suburb on Monday night, was a tornado or microburst.

A roof has been ripped off this house in East Bunbury during a storm on Monday night. (ABC South West WA: Madigan Landry)

Ms Corrin was washing dishes when the roof tore away just after 8pm on Tuesday.

"[I was] completely terrified, to be honest," she said.

"It was almost like the entire roof got lifted off and then placed back down.

"There was water gushing everywhere from the rain and all the pipes and everything -- it was just pouring everywhere."

Ms Corrin described witnessing her roof 'lift off' her home. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Ms Corrin said she was in shock in the moments after the gust struck.

"I was kind of stuck in place for a moment before I kicked into action mode," she said.

" I didn't really know what to do because the entire house seemed like it was falling apart. "

Gone in an instant

Ms Corrin said the storm was deafening.

"At the time the wind sounded like a jet plane coming in like for landing on the house almost," she said.

"Then it was just a lot of banging and crashing and everything just went with it, it was all just instant.

"It happened in mere seconds."

Ms Corrin had just minutes to gather essential items for her and her two children before leaving the unsafe structure. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Ms Corrin said she, her partner and their two children, aged four and five, would be staying with family for the foreseeable future.

"It's a bit crowded so just trying to figure it out," she said.

"We're all just stuck in a room with some family, but safe and sound compared to the other house."

Neighbours heard roof ripped away

Marta Cholkowski lives in the house opposite Ms Corrin and her family and heard the roof being torn away.

Marta Cholkowski says the storm was 'pretty scary' as it blew through. (ABC South West WA: Madigan Landry)

"It was like a really loud, loud, loud like a scraping noise. I wasn't even sure what it was," Ms Cholkowski said.

"All of a sudden the noise and then the flash of light — all the lights, everything went out, including the TV.

"There was actually a powerline streaming across the road — it was quite dangerous."

SES kept busy

Bunbury's State Emergency Service brigade responded to eight calls for help as a result of the storm.

SES volunteer Chris Widmer said there was little they could do.

"The roof structure was gone, the house was unsafe, there was powerlines through the [house]," she said.

"All we could do was offer up some plastic bags so they could gather the possessions and cover them up to keep the rain off."

SES say they responded to eight calls for help the night of the storm. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Mr Widmer said the other calls for assistance were primarily from neighbouring properties.

"The other damage was because of the debris from that property did get thrown into other properties," he said.

"And every property that got hit produced another six or seven missiles and went to someone else's house."

World.title: Iran's meme factory is using 'the weapons of their enemy' to embarrass Trump
World.content:
The video opens on Donald Trump sitting at his desk in the Oval Office. One hand is held to his head, the other grips a mobile phone, about to blast a late-night rant across Truth Social.

Next, we see two jet fighters speeding along a runway before launching in a coordinated manoeuvre against a moonlit sky. The two pilots stare ahead, preparing for battle.

The AI-generated video is set in the animation style of the popular Lego Movie, with a suspenseful soundtrack you would find in a Hollywood blockbuster.

It's one of many pop-culture-steeped videos and memes that have gained momentum on social media in the past month for being deeply critical of Israel and the United States's war in Iran.

Iran war live updates: For the latest news on the Middle East crisis, read our blog.

A small media outfit by the name of Explosive Media said it was behind the Lego videos.

The group claimed it was "totally independent" of the Iranian regime, but a representative admitted to the BBC that Tehran was a "customer".

The clips have been re-shared by Iranian regime accounts, and some have even found their way into the messaging of US protesters opposed to Mr Trump's war in Iran.

Propaganda watchers have coined terms for this content: meme warfare or meme trafficking. In the US, it's known by another title, Lego-ganda.

Most agree it's a clear indication of a new front that has opened up in the war, one fought not with weapons, but with AI tools.

"[The video creators are] taking what's posted seriously online and then turning it into something fun to look at," Nancy Snow, an American communications professor and author who studies propaganda, told the ABC.

The consistent undertone of the videos is impossible to miss: Iran is the underdog in its fight against the United States.

"If you can control the narrative, you can really control the atmosphere and the mood," Professor Snow said.

In AI-era warfare, technological advancements are giving rise to new storytelling methods that can be distributed online in real time at scale.

And analysts say the growth of this type of propaganda is a powerful example of how state actors are attempting to influence not just their domestic populations, but the public opinion of their rivals, with a view to winning the narrative battle in the war.

Iran's meme warfare makes joke of Trump

Explosive Media's first foray into meme warfare occurred last year during the 12-day war, a representative told US media.

By the time the conflict returned at the end of February, their team, which the representative described as "student-led with a background in social activism", was "ready, plans in place, engines revving — and, by day two, the Lego-style videos were back in action".

Explosive Media has created Lego-style clips of Donald Trump and others throughout the war. (Supplied: X/Explosive Media)

The clear target of its videos is Mr Trump, who is regularly mocked and portrayed in an unflattering light, sometimes with his pants on fire or profusely sweating.

One of the earlier videos the group released shows a panicked Mr Trump ordering an air strike after looking over the "Epstein File" alongside Satan.

It is one of many pointed references to the trove of documents related to investigations into the convicted sex offender and former friend of Mr Trump, in an apparent effort to embarrass the US president.

Another video shows the commander-in-chief crying while eating a taco, a nod to the refrain that "Trump always chickens out (TACO)".

News events, both past and present, are regularly sprinkled throughout the videos, including the recent ceasefire deal and Mr Trump's declaration the Strait of Hormuz is open.

Explosive Media's videos have accrued tens of thousands of likes and millions of views on platforms including TikTok, Instagram, and X. The group has also been joined by other creators, including PersiaBoi.

Analysts say the Iranian videos are a form of slopaganda, a combination of slop — unwanted AI-generated content such as memes, video, or text — and propaganda.

But unlike propaganda of the past, which might have taken a week or two months to prepare, the slopaganda distributed throughout the Iran war is being generated quickly and at a greater scale.

"Information warfare has been around ever since there's been warfare. But this is a new manifestation of it, and it's fast. It reaches people that wouldn't otherwise have been reached," Mark Alfano, a computer science expert and associate professor of philosophy at Macquarie University, told the ABC.

"It's very compelling … It's pretty catchy. And these videos are getting dropped once or twice a day at this point and seem to be responding to the events of the day."

The Lego-style videos have attracted a large audience online. (Supplied: X/Explosive Media)

Traditionally, propaganda is targeted at a domestic population, but Dr Alfano explained this "savvy team of maybe a dozen guys" was producing propaganda not for Iranians, but for "Americans and probably Western Europeans".

"The audio is in English, not Farsi," he said.

The use of Lego animation was also quite deliberate, according to Dr Alfano.

"If you put something in a language that people have known since they were five years old, then it's compelling and familiar in a way that is likely to have more influence," he said.

Using 'the weapons of their enemies against them'

Iran's embassies have engaged in other forms of meme warfare throughout the conflict. In a coordinated response to Mr Trump's expletive-laden threat to open the Strait of Hormuz in early April, the social media pages of embassies based in countries including South Africa and New Delhi shared anti-Trump memes on their pages.

The Iranian embassy in Zimbabwe said on X: "We've lost the keys."

In another video shared by the Iranian embassy in South Africa, an AI-generated Mr Trump plays the keyboard and sings: "I will never give you up."

Professor Snow said this was how sophisticated propaganda worked, by incorporating "entertainment value" to shut down the "critical thinking" of its readers or viewers.

"It gets right to the heart of the matter: US bad, Israel bad, and … Iran is the underdog," she said.

"These videos have played an inordinate role in how we're talking about this war in Iran. And so it is setting a mood."

Dr Alfano noted that the creators of the Lego videos and other Iranian propaganda were using tools that were likely "developed and deployed in data centres in the United States".

"So, the resources of the United States are literally being used against the Trump administration right now," he added.

"They just use the weapons of their enemy against them."

The result, Dr Alfano explained, was a "much more volatile information environment" at a time when "public opinion is already on the knife's edge".

"That can be extremely powerful," he said.

"In the same way that the closing of the Strait of Hormuz by small boats with bazookas on them … is still effective, so can this kind of information warfare shape both domestic and international opinion in a way that could be decisive."

The US's 'lack of narrative coherence'

The information war isn't limited to Iran. The US has waged its own propaganda battle throughout its campaign, using pop-culture references and video games to reach more online users.

Mr Trump is part of this machine. And he has shown a willingness to deploy AI content in the past to suit his messaging.

Sometimes it has worked, sometimes it hasn't, analysts say, pointing to the recent controversy over a meme Mr Trump shared, which depicted him as a Jesus-like figure. The US president said he thought the image portrayed him as a "doctor".

Donald Trump posted the image on social media, then deleted it soon after. (Truth Social: Donald Trump)

"It's so unbelievable," Professor Snow said.

Part of the criticism may be a reflection of how people are feeling about a conflict that is costing more lives by the moment. But Dr Alfano has also pointed to "a lack of narrative coherence" in some of the US' propaganda throughout the campaign.

Official US accounts have taken to splicing clips from sports and video games and inserting them into real footage of military strikes before distributing them online.

Those involved in creating the videos have told US media they have proven effective in drawing attention and connecting with young people, but analysts disagree.

"It's unclear who you're supposed to sympathise with, who you're supposed to see as the good guy or the bad guy," Dr Alfano said.

He explained there was a big difference between slicing together scenes from famous movies and TV shows, and the storytelling of the Iranian propagandists, which responds to and narrates current events in short 2-minute videos.

Trump's 'AI Jesus' post sparks backlash Donald Trump is criticised by religious sections of his supporter base after publishing, then deleting, the image, but the US president says: "I thought it was me as a doctor."

The US videos have drawn criticism, including from some former US military officials, for trivialising a war in which more than a dozen US service members have died.

"It just seems detached from reality," Lieutenant General Ben Hodges, a retired two-star general who commanded US troops in Europe during former US president Barack Obama's second term, told Politico.

"Our allies look at this, and they wonder, 'What the hell is going on?' It doesn't look like we're serious."

Professor Snow, who worked at the US Information Agency in Washington in the 1990s, said it appeared as if the US was "losing the propaganda war, both domestically and internationally", in part because "too many state actors are leading the propaganda campaign through their messaging".

"We get inundated with information about Israel and the United States from the top constantly. And so there is this sort of fatigue from all of that," she said.

Propaganda is successful when it has a clear message, analysts say, and when there is a great deal of support for the military campaign. Professor Snow said that was not the case in the US.

"This is not what [Mr Trump's supporters] bargained for," she said.

"This is something that's impacting every home … in the US, [and] around the world too, people … don't want this type of war."

The story that wins is the one that people are going to remember, Professor Snow says, and when it comes to war, this is what underpins the battle for control of the narrative.

"It's about winning the story and winning the narrative. And this is just the next iteration of that," she said.

While she believes Iran has had more success with its messaging than America, the war is far from over.

Even after the conflict ends, the meme warfare proliferating online over the past few months is set to impact everyone.

"The genie is out of the bottle … there's no going back," she said.

World.title: 'How many beers have you had?': Flood evacuees claim racial profiling
World.content:
Evacuees from remote Northern Territory communities say they are being treated "like prisoners" by security guards at emergency accommodation in Batchelor, set up after catastrophic flooding forced them from their homes last month.

Homes inundated and locals band together: NT floods in pictures Many regions across the Northern Territory were submerged by flooding through March this year. Here is some of the most dramatic footage from the extreme weather event, right across the Top End.

Residents from Palumpa and Daly River / Nauiyu have been living at the Batchelor Institute of Indigenous Tertiary Education, south of Darwin, for the past month, with private security guards stationed at the entry and exit.

Daly River resident James Parry, who has been living in emergency accommodation since March, said evacuees felt racially profiled when coming and going.

"If you walk down to the store and come back, the first thing they ask you is 'How many beers have you had today?'" he said.

"You try and tell them 'I haven't been at the pub' and that's where the conflict starts.

" They're treating us like prisoners, it's terrible. "

Mr Parry said the security guards searched evacuees' cars and bags every time someone exited or entered the premises, leaving residents feeling vulnerable.

James Parry says security guards are routinely searching evacuees bags and cars. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"You sign back in, your car gets searched — everybody gets told to get out of the car, and they search your bag and your private stuff, which is not right," he said.

Another resident, who did not want to be named, shared similar experiences.

"They're invading our privacy and we're not doing anything," she said.

" Even if they just let you out for like five, 10 minutes in the morning, they still ask you if you're a resident or if you have alcohol in the car — who serves alcohol at 8 o'clock in the morning? "

She said as the weeks went on, fewer people were attending meetings convened by the centre.

One resident sheltering at the evacuation hub shared their story with the ABC on the condition of anonymity. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"Everyone turns up expecting to hear some good news about home, but we hear little about home and more about the rules and what not to do around here," she said.

In a statement, a spokesperson said the NT government took concerns raised by evacuees seriously and the measures in place were designed to ensure safety.

"Security measures are in place to maintain a safe, respectful and alcohol-free environment, and may include bag or vehicle checks on entry," they said.

“These measures are designed to protect residents and staff and to ensure the site remains safe for everyone."

Aboriginal organisations snubbed

Aboriginal Peak Organisations NT (APONT) offered to send volunteers to assist NT government workers at the evacuation centre more than a week ago, but says it received no response.

Late last week, the NT government instead announced students on placement from Charles Darwin University's social work undergraduate degree would assist at Batchelor.

The emergency accommodation was established in Batchelor after last month's floods to support evacuees still unable to return home. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Speaking at a meeting of flood evacuees outside the centre on Monday, Northern Land Council (NLC) chair Matthew Ryan questioned the NT government's logic.

"We need to engage the right people in the community, which is the APONT group," he said.

"Why aren't we utilising them to interpret and to work with the community closely?

" Why get university students who'll have problems understanding my people? "

Mr Ryan said NLC staff had routinely been barred from entering the site, even after pre-arranging their visits, a claim backed up by Aboriginal Housing NT chief executive Leeanne Caton.

Matthew Ryan says Northern Land Council staff have been blocked from entering the evacuation centre. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"I went down to the centre [on Monday] and I was asked if I was from the NLC," she said.

"I said 'No, I'm not', and I was allowed to go in, but apparently if you're the NLC you need to give 24 hours' notice before you can come down here — what's going on?"

After six weeks at the centre, one resident said she was disheartened by the lack of access for the land council.

"They're keeping everybody in the dark," she said.

" Are they afraid that NLC are going to say something they don't want everyone to know? "

The NT government spokesperson said it was aware of correspondence offering support and would continue to work with Aboriginal-controlled organisations.

In response to the NLC's access claims, the spokesperson said security decisions were made to protect residents' privacy.

"We are balancing requests from organisations with feedback from residents, who have told us they want to limit the number of visitors on site during this time," they said.

"Where onsite access is not appropriate, alternative options have been offered, including facilitating meetings with residents at offsite locations."

Uncertainty over Palumpa return plan

Evacuees from Palumpa told a meeting of stakeholders they had questions about a plan to repatriate some members of the remote Indigenous community from as soon as Wednesday.

Community members say they were told about the development on Monday morning, having previously believed they would be staying in Batchelor for several more weeks.

Residents living at the shelter want more transparency regarding repatriation plans. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

While many have been longing to return home, the announcement has raised concerns about the liveability of the community when they get back.

"It's a health and safety issue, there could be mould build-up within the houses because of the moisture and the wet season," Mr Ryan said.

"Food security, what's that going to look like?"

Ms Caton said the repatriation process had been marred by poor communication.

Leeanne Caton says Palumpa residents were surprised to hear about the latest repatriation plan. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"There is no flow of communication to these people," she said.

"We heard [yesterday] that Palumpa residents might be going back on Wednesday, well that was news to them."

Arnhem Land Progress Association chief executive Alastair King said he was surprised by Monday's repatriation announcement, having recently assessed the damage at Palumpa.

Remote community's bid to relocate progresses after '30 years of asking' Flood-affected residents from Daly River are in talks with the NT government about moving the community to higher ground, with a land donation offered up.

"The store has been a metre under water, all of the stock is gone, the chiller freezer's all turned to liquid, so that's a biohazard and has to be disposed of," he said.

"The store manager's house had water three-quarters of the way up the walls, so that whole house has got to be gutted because of the black mould."

Mr King said if residents were to return to the community in coming days, there would be serious limitations on what goods and services could be delivered.

"There's no clinic, no school, no essential services except for power, water and sewer," he said.

The NT government spokesperson said provision for the delivery of school, health and store services in Palumpa had been established, and the government had consulted with elders prior to the announcement.

They said the repatriation was still expected to go ahead today, subject to final safety checks.

"Returns will happen in stages, starting with residents whose homes are ready and safe," they said.

World.title: Leicester City relegated to third tier just five years after FA Cup glory
World.content:
Former Premier League champion Leicester City will be playing in the third tier of English football next season.

Leicester, which sealed the unlikeliest title win of the Premier League era in 2016 at odds of 5,000 to 1, needed a victory overnight to maintain hope of avoiding relegation, but drew 2-2 with Hull.

The Midlands club, which also won the FA Cup in 2021 and played in England's top flight last season, is second to last in the second-tier Championship.

Relegation comes after Leicester was docked six points in February for breaching the English Football League's financial rules when it earned promotion in the 2023-24 season.

Earlier this month, it lost its bid to overturn that punishment, leaving it mired in the relegation zone.

It is a dramatic fall after Leicester's fairytale-like title triumph 10 years ago.

It had spent the 2014-15 season battling relegation from the top flight and only an unlikely winning run in the final weeks of that campaign saved them.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

What followed was a remarkable title charge that saw it finish 10 points clear of Arsenal at the top of the standings.

In 142 years of existence, Leicester has played just one season in the third tier of English football, winning the League One title in 2008-09 and was promoted back to the Championship.

Slipping down the football pyramid is costly mainly because of the decreasing broadcast revenue.

In the 2023-24 season, League One clubs' average total revenue was $17 million, which was about one-quarter of Championship clubs' average revenue, according to Deloitte.

The average revenue for Premier League clubs that season was $422 million.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Rates bill shock forecast as councils struggle with debt
World.content:
Local governments in WA are increasingly unable to pay their bills amid growing levels of debt, according to a financial health scorecard.

The Auditor General's report on local government audits for the 2025 financial year was tabled to parliament last week, revealing many local governments were facing financial pressure.

The result could be higher rates and delays to projects, the WA Local Government Association (WALGA) said.

More debts than assets

Auditor General Caroline Spencer said the shires with the worst asset-to-debt ratios were Coolgardie, Derby-West Kimberley, Irwin and Victoria Plains.

Caroline Spencer says numerous local governments are facing financial pressure. (ABC News: James Carmody)

"They have more short-term debts than they have cash in the bank, essentially," Ms Spencer said.

The Wheatbelt shire of Victoria Plains said the report only reflected a snapshot in time and its financial positions would improve.

"What cash you have on any given day is up and down," Victoria Plains chief executive Sean Fletcher said.

"It's not a trend or anything like that, so there's no concern there."

Legacy projects blow out

Mr Fletcher and Irwin Shire president Isabelle Scott said legacy issues and cost blow outs on big projects were behind their debt levels.

They included a heavily-delayed road intersection project in Victoria Plains, and the repurchasing of road-building equipment by the Shire of Irwin.

Ms Scott said in recent years the shire had been forced to pay for essential projects such as acquiring a medical centre when the previous private GP service closed.

The shire continues to heavily support a private GP service at the site.

"We have made some large conscious decisions to borrow money in order to invest in the community," Ms Scott said.

"It does mean we have to be careful going forward and we will be looking to make sure that our debt is reduced."

Both local government leaders said fuel costs had been identified as a concern for the future, and they were factoring the costs into their next budgets.

Push for fairer funding

Ms Scott said the Shire of Irwin was often rejected for financial assistance grants and received less funding than other local governments of a similar size.

A private medical centre in Dongara is heavily supported by the Shire of Irwin. (Supplied: Isabelle Scott)

She said she was told Irwin did not meet the measures of disadvantage that were used by the Local Government Grants Commission.

A Department of Local Government spokesperson said the shire received $665,000 in grants in 2025-26, based on its "revenue capacity, expenditure, need, and relative disadvantage".

It said allocations could be appealed, and Irwin had done so in the past.

Pressures increasing

WALGA president Mark Irwin said regional local governments in particular were expected to deliver more projects and services with limited revenue options.

Mark Irwin says most local governments would be forced to adopt inflation increases. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

He said local governments were likely to pass inflated expenses onto ratepayers.

"Most local governments, if they don't decide to at least adopt the CPI increase, they'll be going backwards," he said.

"Then they'll decide what they can and can't do this year, and work out their rates accordingly.

"We could see some local governments put projects off for a year."

Mr Irwin said WALGA was helping smaller local governments look into shared service models for some services to split costs.

World.title: US authorities probe possible ChatGPT involvement in university shooting
World.content:
US authorities are investigating if there was any criminal behaviour involving interactions between Open AI's ChatGPT app and a man accused of killing two people and injuring six others in a shooting at Florida State University (FSU) last year.

Florida Attorney-General James Uthmeier said prosecutors had carried out an initial review of chat logs between ChatGPT and the alleged gunman, Phoenix Ikner, to determine if the AI app aided or abetted the crime.

"This criminal investigation will determine whether OpenAI bears criminal responsibility for ChatGPT's actions in the shooting at Florida State University last year," Mr Uthmeier said at a news conference in Tampa, on Tuesday, local time.

Two dead as police officer's son fires old service weapon at US university Five people were hospitalised when the gunman rampaged through Florida State University, shooting at students.

Florida's Office of Statewide Prosecution has subpoenaed OpenAI for records of its policies and training materials regarding threats to harm others, and for its policies on reporting "possible past, present, or future crime", according to the attorney-general's office.

OpenAI spokeswoman Kate Waters called the FSU shooting a tragedy but said the company had no responsibility.

The company proactively shared information with law enforcement and continued to cooperate with investigators, she said on Tuesday.

"In this case, ChatGPT provided factual responses to questions with information that could be found broadly across public sources on the internet, and it did not encourage or promote illegal or harmful activity," Ms Waters said in an email.

At least two people died in the shooting in April 2025. (AP: Kate Payne )

Mr Ikner faces two counts of first-degree murder and several counts of attempted first-degree murder over the shooting at the university campus in Florida's capital city.

Investigators allege Mr Ikner, who is the stepson of a local sheriff's deputy, used his stepmother's former service weapon to carry out the shooting.

Prosecutors in the case say they intend to seek the death penalty.

AP

World.title: Eczema medication costing families thousands due to PBS age limit
World.content:
Playing rugby league with his friends is one of Tanner Hosie's favourite things to do, but there was a time when, due to a debilitating skin condition, this was not possible.

The 10-year-old boy from Narrandera in southern New South Wales was diagnosed with severe eczema at six months old.

"I couldn't stop scratching, but whenever you scratched, it hurt more," he said.

Kasey-Rae Hosie says it was hard to watch her son not have a normal childhood. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato )

"As an active little boy wanting to play outside, he could kick the footy with his siblings and come back inside, and he'd be raw from head to toe," his mum, Kasey-Rae Hosie, said.

Eczema is an incurable immune dysregulation skin disease that causes red, dark brown or purple skin lesions, which are dry, scaly and painful, and prone to bleeding and infection.

It was not uncommon for Tanner Hosie to be covered in scars and blood because of constantly scratching his skin. (Supplied: Kasey-Rae Hosie )

Despite trying everything from steroid creams to bleach baths, little eased his pain.

"Seeing him wake up with blood all through his bed and stuck to his sheets — the process has been emotional and exhausting," Ms Hosie said.

Hospital visits were normal for Tanner when his eczema was out of control. (Supplied: Kasey-Rae Hosie)

But two years ago, his dermatologist suggested a medication that changed his life.

Dupilumab, used to treat chronic inflammatory conditions and given via bi-weekly or monthly injections, improved his condition within weeks.

"I could play outside, kick the footy, and ride my bike," Tanner said.

Tanner Hosie can now kick the footy around without major eczema flare ups. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato )

While the medication changed his life, for children under 12, it can cost families up to $1,600 a month for a script, making it inaccessible to many.

High cost for relief

For those over the age of 12, the medication is listed on the Pharmaceutical Benefit Scheme (PBS) and costs $25 a month.

Tanner was only eight when his doctor suggested he give it a try.

"You just have to make it work, you don't have a choice in the matter," Ms Hosie said.

Before Dupilumab, eczema flare-ups were Tanner Hosie's norm. (Supplied: Kasey-Rae Hosie )

It was around this time in 2024 that Tanner lost his father, leaving Ms Hosie as the lone breadwinner for her four children.

Due to her financial circumstances, Ms Hosie was able to access the medication through the pharmaceutical company's compassionate funding.

However, the condition for this funding is a review of eligibility every six months.

"There is that nervous factor," Ms Hosie said.

" What if the company's policies or regulations have changed, and they say no? "

Now, Ms Hosie is fighting for changes to the PBS, both for her son and for others who are unable to afford the life-changing medicine.

Lifelong damage

Roughly 10 per cent of the population — 2.8 million Australians — are impacted by eczema.

Li Chuen Wong says she does not understand why PBS funding for Dupilumab for children under 12 years of age has not been approved. (Supplied: Dr Li Chuen Wong )

Li-Chuen Wong is a paediatric dermatologist and said that, due to the severe nature of eczema, patients cannot just stop using medication without support.

"At the moment, it's labelled as indefinite and ongoing treatment," Dr Wong said.

"However, in my experience, I have got patients that are able to wean off the medication."

She said if not dealt with, comorbidities like asthma, hay fever, food allergies, anxiety, depression and ADHD can be common for people who have suffered from severe eczema.

"These comorbidities have to be addressed aggressively because in young children, they can have a long-term impact," Dr Wong said.

"There is this window of opportunity where if you have severe eczema and are given treatments such as dupilumab in the early years, around two to three years of age, even younger, it can disease-modify."

Dr Wong said she does not understand why the drug has not already been approved on the PBS for children.

"It's really distressing as a clinician to know that there are treatments that are available and used overseas from six months of age," she said.

"We know it's safe, we know it's effective, and we know that it's going to work for our little kids with severe disease."

In March 2022, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee (PBAC) recommended dupilumab for severe atopic dermatitis for patients under 12 years of age.

The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing said the next step, which required support documentation from the pharmaceutical company, Sanofi, did not occur.

Sanofi said it is providing an updated proposal for the PBAC to consider at an advisory committee meeting in July this year that will reassess the drug for children under 12.

Push for change

Eczema Support Australia recently launched its Save our Skin (SOS) for kids with Eczema campaign, advocating to lower the age for PBS funding.

Melanie Funk is pushing for a change to PBS funding for children under the age of 12. (Supplied: Eczema Support Australia )

The organisation's managing director, Melanie Funk, said when Dupilumab was first listed on the PBS in 2021 for people over 12, they expected younger children to soon follow.

"I know there's lots of complex things for them to talk about, but for families who have just been waiting, they can't wait any longer," she said.

"We've had families talk to us about setting up GoFundMe pages, remortgaging their home, and some families even considering moving to another country where they might be able to get more affordable access.

"These are decisions in Australia that no family should have to make for the well-being of their severely unwell child."

For children like Tanner, the medication has given him a normal childhood again.

Kasey-Rae Hosie just wants her son to have a normal childhood. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato )

"I was sad because I couldn't run around and play," he said.

"It (Dupilumab) really helped me when I had really bad eczema, I got way better — I now play softball at lunch, or play markers up, and football."

World.title: ‘Don’t bother coming back’: Kyle’s alleged rant at Jackie ‘O’
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing ‘Don’t bother coming back’: Kyle’s alleged rant at Jackie ‘O’ Calum Jaspan April 22, 2026 — 10:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Kyle Sandilands allegedly “repeatedly bullied” Jackie ‘O’ Henderson in the workplace before their partnership disintegrated on live radio in February, with new court documents alleging he told his co-star to “get your f---ing shit together” off air in September 2025. Sandilands is alleged to have told Henderson he had carried the show by himself for more than a year during the exchange, which forms part of the defence by radio network KIIS’ corporate parent to the star’s claims that was detailed in Federal Court documents filed late on Tuesday. Kyle Sandilands and Jackie ‘O’ Henderson are embroiled in a messy legal squabble. Michael Howard Both Sandilands and Henderson are suing their former network after it tore up their contracts, which were worth a combined $200 million over 10 years, in two stages in March. The documents filed this week allege that after a disagreement between the pair on air on September 10 2025, verbal conflict allegedly escalated off-air. “Don’t f---ing bother coming back until you’ve got your f---ing shit together like a normal person. I’ve been carrying the whole show for a f---ing year… I’m just left here with a limp d-ck in my hand,” Sandilands allegedly said according to the documents.



“Kyle, that’s a bit rough. Like, f---en hell, I haven’t done anything to cop it,” Henderson said following the spray from Sandilands, who said he had repeatedly tried to bring up her lack of engagement on the show and “rescue the show”. “Too bad if it’s rough, that’s what I’ve been dealing with you for the last 12 months. Not interested. Not connected,” Sandilands said. “You wanna know the truth, here’s the truth. Today’s the first day you’ve ever paid any attention or had to carry anything in the opener, and it’s all shit,” Sandilands said, according to the documents. ARN alleges that after complaints made about Sandilands in mid-September, and after the company tried to follow up on those complaints, Henderson’s manager Gemma O’Neill told KIIS station manager Derek Bargwanna that no further action was required. The radio network has defended its decision to axe both stars in the series of documents, arguing that Sandilands had destroyed his relationship with Henderson and that he had breached his contract through a persistent course of workplace bullying and harassment of Henderson. It said that Sandilands breached its own work, health and safety policies, code of conduct and respect in the workplace policies. It also alleges his actions toward Henderson in February breached the NSW Workplace Health and Safety Act.

World.title: Big aromatics, zero fuss: Dazzle the table with this one-tray coconut curry fish
World.content:
Step 1 Combine the brown rice and 2 cups of water in a saucepan over high heat; once boiling, reduce to low, cover, and simmer for 25 minutes. Remove from the heat and let it sit, covered, for 10 minutes to finish steaming before spreading it out to cool.

Step 2 While the rice cooks, whisk the curry paste, coconut milk, half the fish sauce and the juice of half the lime directly in a shallow roasting tray. Cut the lemongrass into 5cm lengths, bruising them with the back of a knife to release their aromatics, and stir them into the coconut mixture.

Step 3 Cut the remaining lime half into slices and stuff them into the snapper cavity. Place the fish into the tray, spoon the sauce over it and season lightly. Roast for 25-30 minutes, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily. At the 15-minute mark, baste the fish with the sauce to prevent it from drying out.

World.title: Apartment or house? What strata does (and doesn’t) cover for landlords
World.content:
Sponsored MoneyInvestingTerri Scheer Landlord Insurance Apartment or house? What strata does (and doesn’t) cover for landlords Sponsored by Terri Scheer Landlord Insurance Nina Hendy April 22, 2026 — 10:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

If you own a property in a strata-titled building, understanding what your strata insurance does and doesn’t cover is essential. And yet, many landlords mistakenly believe that residential strata insurance covers everything – and that if all else fails, a tenant’s bond will plug the gaps. Put simply, strata insurance is designed to cover the building’s structure and common areas. It may also cover certain shared property (such as appliances, equipment and furniture in communal spaces, depending on the policy and the scheme. Many landlords mistakenly assume strata insurance covers all property-related risks. iStock Across Australia, strata legislation and scheme by-laws generally require the owners corporation (also known as the body corporate) of a strata property to hold building insurance for common property. For landlords, it plays an important role in protecting shared property assets – including those that may not be top of mind, such as damage to foyers, stairwells, gardens and some shared security systems. Depending on the policy, strata insurance may also respond to certain events that may impact the building structure (for example, storm-related damage) and may include liability cover for incidents on common property, as well as cover for some legal costs.



While the safety net that is strata insurance offers considerable peace of mind, it doesn’t cover everything. For landlords, understanding potential gaps can help reduce the financial impact of an unexpected event. What’s covered? Most properties on a strata title will be covered by a strata insurance policy arranged by the owners’ corporation. Depending on the structure of the scheme, this can include apartment complexes, a small group of units, duplexes, low-rise boutique apartments and certain retirement villages. Strata insurance can extend to common property items such as property fences, driveways, and some standalone structures on common property (for example, a shared garage), but what’s included depends on the policy.



The joint owners or body corporate of a building are responsible for arranging strata building insurance, with the cost typically shared by owners through strata levies. The intention is to spread risk across the scheme rather than leaving individual owners to fund major building-related losses on their own. What’s not covered? As a landlord, items inside your lot (your individual apartment or unit), such as curtains, carpet, floorboards, kitchen or bathroom counters or light fittings, may not be covered by the strata building insurance policy. The same goes for public liability – strata insurance focuses on incidents on common property, rather than on the risk that a visitor or tradesperson injures themselves while inside your unit, exposing you personally to the risk of a lawsuit. It also doesn’t cover you for loss of rent if your property becomes inaccessible or uninhabitable. This is where landlord insurance comes into play: a separate policy, tailored to the risks of your property investment. Understanding how strata insurance differs from landlord insurance can help you decide what cover you may need. Being underinsured can leave property owners significantly out of pocket for repairs or rebuilding after an insured event.



The problem of maintaining adequate insurance cover on your investment property amid a cost-of-living crisis is critical, but many fall short. A Terri Scheer survey in January found the most common policy held by landlord investors is non-specialist home insurance (59 per cent), followed by landlord insurance (54 per cent). Finding a policy When deciding which provider to go with, it can be useful to look for a specialist in the landlord insurance space able to offer options that cover the specific needs of your investment property. For example, landlord insurance specialist Terri Scheer offers policies designed to address risks associated with owning a rental property. Established in 1995, the company is Australia’s leading landlord insurance specialist with decades of experience. And as far as strata insurance goes, it’s important to be familiar with your policy – and its limits. Premiums are typically calculated based on factors such as building size and condition, previous claims history, age of the property, value of the insured building and whether you’ve signed up for any optional extras.

World.title: Boy, 15, among alleged kidnappers of Sydney rapper’s bodyguard
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Boy, 15, among alleged kidnappers of Sydney rapper’s bodyguard Daniel Lo Surdo Updated April 22, 2026 — 9:45am ,first published 9:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The five-person crew behind the alleged gunpoint abduction of a Sydney rapper’s bodyguard has been charged by the state’s anti-gang detectives, a day after the man was snatched from a Guildford home in the latest targeted attack on the Alameddine crime family. Emilio Chalhoub, 32, was allegedly beaten by the group of masked men after being kidnapped from his family’s Guildford home on Monday night, triggering an expansive police operation that led detectives to a safe house by the Hume Highway in Casula, where the group fled before being arrested in a nearby street. Chalhoub was recovered in Casula about an hour after he was bundled into his own car, and was hospitalised with facial injuries. Rapper Ay Huncho, whose legal name is Ali Younes. Instagram Chalhoub is the bodyguard of rapper Ali Younes, aka Ay Huncho, an alleged senior member of the Alameddine organised crime network. Last year, Chalhoub was the intended target of an attack at his Guildford home in which his 62-year-old father was allegedly stabbed by two intruders – a 15-year-old boy and a 22-year-old man – at the height of an internal conflict within the fractured Alameddine network. Luke Manuatu, 22, Anaru Warren, 22, Hikairo Mohi, 21, Harley Sorbello, 21, and a 15-year-old boy have been charged with a raft of offences following Chalhoub’s abduction.



Related Article Updated

Crime Sydney rapper’s bodyguard snatched from family home in alleged late-night abduction This includes kidnapping and causing actual bodily harm, possessing an unauthorised firearm, wearing a face covering with intent to commit an indictable offence, destroying property greater than $5000 using fire, and aggravated use of a car armed with a weapon. The four men were refused bail to appear at Liverpool Local Court on Wednesday, while the 15-year-old will front a Children’s Court on Wednesday. Police said a pistol, a baseball bat and other weapons were found inside the Casula property, where Chalhoub’s alleged captors tied his hands and feet together and assaulted him. Forensics officers have also examined Chalhoub’s burnt-out ute found at Villawood, and a hatchback police believe was used to ferry him to the Casula property.



NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said detectives were having “great success” in its targeting of organised crime under Taskforce Falcon, established last year amid spiralling violence linked to the fracturing of the Alameddine network, as they confront a “different organised crime environment”. Police conduct a line search outside the Casula property on Tuesday. Sam Mooy “We’re seeing young people predominantly being contracted online to conduct very serious criminal activity, be it murder, be it kidnapping, be it drive-by shootings – as a police force, that’s why we’re making such a concerted effort,” Lanyon told 2GB on Wednesday morning. “The fact that it’s so brazen is why we take it so seriously, why we have scaled up and why we have such a dedicated approach to organised crime.” Younes, the cousin of the Alameddine’s Lebanon-based patriarch Rafat Alameddine, was the believed target of a foiled attack in western Sydney earlier this month, resulting in the arrests of three men and seizure of two firearms. Detectives have repeatedly warned Younes and Chalhoub of threats to their safety.



Police are investigating if the alleged kidnapping is related to the foiled plot to target Younes, or the ongoing conflicts involving the Alameddine network. Former allies and emerging groups vying for control of Sydney’s underworld have targeted Alameddine members and associates for the past 18 months. Several senior members who have fled to the Middle East are alleged to be involved in the large-scale importation of cocaine and methamphetamine into Australia. World.title: WA news LIVE: Man recovering in Perth hospital after crocodile attack
World.content:
A West Australian man continues to recover in hospital from his injuries after being attacked by a large crocodile at the weekend.

The victim, Jimmy, aged in his 20s, was sleeping in a swag on a beach at a popular camping spot about 100 kilometres north of Broome when he was attacked.

Loading

Parks and Wildlife say it’s the second incident in the Kimberley region this year.

Jimmy, who was flown to Royal Perth Hospital for surgery, says he is grateful for the well-wishes.

He is currently in a stable condition.

World.title: 2026 election: Lan Pham moves higher than two fellow MPs in Greens list
World.content:
Photo: VNP / Phil Smith

The Green Party has confirmed its candidate list for the election, with some current MPs bumped up slightly compared to an earlier draft.

That initial list was put together by delegates, to then be voted on by the wider party membership, then reviewed and approved for publication by a group of party representatives.

The final version has Lan Pham leapfrogging Parliamentary colleagues Hūhana Lyndon and Lawrence Xu-Nan.

After the draft in March also had Steve Abel - ranked 9th for the 2023 election - dropping down to 14th, he is now back up to 12th, swapping places with former Environment Canterbury chairperson Craig Aaron Pauling.

Photo: RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Lawyer and Treaty of Waitangi activist Tania Waikato - who put herself forward to represent Te Pāti Māori's co-leaders and MP Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke at the Privileges Committee after the Treaty Principles Bill haka - has moved up two spots to 13th.

That is a critical spot at this point with the most recent public poll - by Verian for 1News - projecting 13 seats for the Greens with 11 percent of the vote.

Scott Willis, who came into Parliament at 12th, was ranked by delegates at 16th but has risen to 15th in the final list.

Their elevation comes at the expense of Auckland Pride co-chair Bhen Goodsir, who has dropped from 13th in the draft to 17th.

Mike Davidson, who entered Parliament at 19th after the resignation of Benjamin Doyle, has returned to that spot after the draft list had him at 22nd.

Heather Te Au-Skipworth - who quit Te Pāti Māori after being replaced for candidacy of the Ikaroa-Rāwhiti seat in 2023 by her cousin Meka Whaitiri, who had jumped ship from Labour - has dropped from 19th to 21st.

Two candidates - Asher Wilson-Goldman and Nathan Hoturoa Gray - have also withdrawn their names, with the party saying this was for personal reasons.
